transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I guess I'm here because my family and, well, pretty much everyone keeps acting like I'm just making things up or imagining it all, which is incredibly frustrating because I am absolutely not imagining it. You see, I've been working as a housekeeper for years, cleaning houses all over town, and lately... well, not just lately, for a while now, I know for a fact that the people from the hospital and some of the folks from the agency have been watching us. 

They've been watching our house, just sitting out there, and they even follow me on my cleaning routes. I'll be driving to my Tuesday house, hauling all my supplies in the trunk, and I can tell they are keeping tabs on me. They're doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. Because he needs me, you know? And I take good care of him, I really do, between all my shifts and the laundry and the cooking, but they just want to catch me slipping up. They want to prove I'm not doing a good enough job with him, and it's just... it's exhausting trying to explain this to people who just look at you like you've lost your mind when the proof is right there on my route every single day. I just want them to leave me be so I can do my work and take care of my home.
It sounds like you have been feeling under a lot of stress with everything going on. Have you ever heard any voices or sounds when no one else was around?

Well, yes, actually. And it's funny you bring that up because my husband, he never hears it, which just makes him think I'm more crazy, but I know what I hear. It usually happens when I'm finally home from work, you know, after I've put away all my cleaning supplies—the bleach, the rags, the mop—and I'm trying to get dinner started or maybe just wiping down the counters one last time. The house will be completely quiet, just dead silent, especially if my husband is resting in the living room. 

And then, right by the kitchen window—the one that looks out over the side yard where the hydrangeas are—I'll hear her. It's a woman's voice. And she doesn't just mumble, doctor. It's not like a whisper or the wind or something you could just brush off. It is clear as day, as if she is standing right there on the other side of the glass, or maybe even right inside the kitchen with me. She'll tell me things I need to do. She'll say, "Check the locks," or she'll tell me to move his pills to a different spot. And I have to listen, because what if they're trying to get in? What if the agency people sent her to test me? So I go and check the deadbolt on the back door, and I make sure his medication organizer is pushed all the way back on the shelf where no one can tamper with it. I try to explain this to my family, that she's warning me or testing me, but they just roll their eyes. But I hear her, doctor. I'm not making it up.

Persistent what, doctor? I'm sorry, you trailed off there. Persistent sadness? Persistent tiredness? Because if you're asking if I've been feeling down or depressed, well, no, not really. I mean, I'm stressed, like I said. Anyone would be stressed if they had a whole agency of people breathing down their neck while they're just trying to scrub baseboards and keep a household running. But depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. 

I actually have quite a bit of energy most days. Too much, sometimes. I'll be up at four in the morning, wide awake, thinking about the schedule for the week, making sure I have enough heavy-duty degreaser for the Johnsons' stove on Thursday, and reorganizing my husband's pill boxes just in case that woman's voice was right about them needing to be moved again. I don't have time to be depressed, doctor. I have to stay vigilant. I have to keep moving. If I stop, if I just sit around feeling sorry for myself, that's exactly when they'll swoop in and say I'm unfit. So, no, I'm not sitting around crying, if that's what you mean. I'm just trying to keep my head above water and keep them from taking my husband away.

Well, let me think. I want to be completely accurate because my family always says I get my dates mixed up, but I know exactly when all of this started. It was... gosh, it’s been about 11 months now. Yes, exactly 11 months. I remember specifically because it was right around the time I was doing the big autumn deep-clean for the Henderson place—they always want the baseboards and the ceiling fans scrubbed down before they have their holiday company over, you know how people get when their in-laws are coming to town. 

And that's when I first noticed the cars parked at the end of our street, just idling there while I was loading my vacuum into the trunk. So the feeling that people from the agency and the hospital are watching us, and then that woman's voice chiming in to tell me to check the locks and move the pills... all of that has been going on for about 11 months now. At first, I thought maybe it was just a coincidence, the cars I mean, just someone lost or looking for an address, but then the voice started right after, maybe a week or two later, right there by the kitchen window with the hydrangeas just like I told you. 

And it hasn't stopped since. Every single month, month after month for 11 solid months, I've had to be on high alert. I'm constantly checking the windows, checking the deadbolts, making sure my husband's routine is perfect while I'm out scrubbing floors and polishing silver for people who don't even appreciate how hard it is to get hard water stains out of marble. And you'd think, doctor, you would really think that after 11 months of watching me run myself ragged keeping a perfect home and doing my job, they'd have enough proof that I'm doing a fine job taking care of him. But no, she's still talking to me, and they're still out there keeping tabs.
